narration.full_text:
In this section, we will delve into the graphical method for solving pairs of linear equations. This method offers a visual understanding of how solutions arise. We will explore three distinct graphical outcomes: intersecting lines, parallel lines, and coincident lines, and understand what each of these scenarios implies about the nature of the solutions.

First, let's consider the scenario where two lines intersect at a single point. This indicates a unique solution for the system of equations. The coordinates of this intersection point represent the values of x and y that satisfy both equations simultaneously. This type of system is known as a consistent system, as it has at least one solution.

Next, we'll look at parallel lines. When two lines are parallel, they never intersect, no matter how far they are extended. Graphically, this means there is no common point between the two lines, and therefore, no solution exists for the system of equations. Such a system is termed an inconsistent system, as it has no solution at all.

Finally, we have the case of coincident lines. This occurs when both equations represent the exact same line. Essentially, one line lies perfectly on top of the other. In this situation, every point on the line is a common solution to both equations. Since there are infinitely many points on a line, this system has infinitely many solutions. This is known as a dependent system, a special type of consistent system.
